title: size vs capacity
concept: Vector manages size (actual number of elements) and capacity (allocated space) separately.

steps.title: Create an empty vector
steps.explanation: The first created vector has size=0, capacity=0. We have not allocated any memory on the heap yet.

steps.title: first push_back
steps.explanation:
Since capacity is 0, new space (usually 1) is allocated in the heap and then elements are added.

size=1, capacity=1.

steps.title: Second push_back — reallocation occurs
steps.explanation:
Since capacity(1) is insufficient, allocate **larger space (usually 2 times)** and copy the existing data.

Old memory is freed. This is Vector’s ‘growth strategy’.

steps.title: Third push_back — reallocate again
steps.explanation:
As capacity(2) is exceeded, new memory of twice the size (4) is allocated again.

**Key**: size=3 but capacity=4. The remaining 1 space will be used without reallocation during the next push_back.

quiz.question: Why is the capacity of a vector greater than its size?
options: Free space to avoid reallocation every time push_back
Capacity is always exactly twice the size
quiz.explanation: If you reserve enough capacity in advance, push_back will mostly complete in O(1). Amortization analysis ensures efficiency.

misconceptions.correct: Normally this would be O(1), but when reallocation occurs, it is O(n) because all existing elements must be copied.
misconceptions.why: However, the reallocation frequency decreases exponentially, becoming O(1) with amortization.

keyTakeaway: vector guarantees the amortized O(1) performance of push_back with a 2x growth strategy.
